strengths: The paper addresses a well-motivated and underexplored question: whether small language models can reliably self-verify under test-time scaling without relying on larger verifier models. The core observation that sLM verification fails primarily on memorization-heavy steps (arithmetic, fact-checking), even after distillation, is an interesting and useful empirical finding.

The proposed method is simple and practical: a binary tool-based filtering stage followed by reward-model scoring, integrated cleanly with both PRMs and generative verifiers, with multi-LoRA distillation from a teacher.

The evaluation is reasonably broad: three small models (360M, 0.5B, 1B), two verifier types, three benchmarks (MATH500, GSM8K, MMLU-Pro), plus useful analyses (category/level breakdown, verifier-size scaling, confusion matrices, data-efficiency of distillation, and case studies of successes and failures).

The headline result (Llama-3.2-1B with T1 surpassing Llama-3.1-8B on MATH500 under best-of-N) is compelling and clearly presented, and the appendices provide sufficient implementation detail (hyperparameters, prompts, distillation data) for reasonable reproducibility.
The limitations are honestly discussed, including the false-negative problem of a rejection-only filter and the restriction to parallel scaling.
weaknesses: Limited novelty. Tool use for verification/reward modeling already exists (e.g., tool-augmented reward modeling, ToRA, PAL-style program-aided verification), and the method is essentially 'filter candidates with code execution/retrieval, then apply an RM.' The framing as a new scaling axis (T1) is somewhat overstated relative to this prior art.

The theoretical analysis is thin. Theorem 5.2 assumes an idealized, perfectly reliable tool, making I(X;θ|P)=0 nearly tautological; the gap between this assumption and reality (the paper itself shows ~10-20% of code-based verifications fail, Table 3) is not bridged. Theorem 5.3 is a standard monotonicity result essentially imported from prior work. The theory also covers only toy tasks (scalar addition) rather than the actual verification setting.

Compute accounting is not fair or transparent. ToolV adds substantial inference cost (generating and executing code, multiple completions, retrieval) that is not counted against the test-time compute budget when claiming 1B beats 8B. A compute-matched comparison against tool-integrated generation or scaled majority voting is missing.

Missing important baselines: tool-integrated generation (generating solutions with code, e.g., ToRA/START-style), larger off-the-shelf verifiers without distillation at matched cost, and self-consistency variants of ToolV. The comparison against the 8B model uses greedy decoding only (N=1), which inflates the scaling narrative.

Several claims and descriptions are imprecise: GSM8K is described as 'graduate-level arithmetic problems' (it is grade-school), weighted best-of-N scoring is not precisely defined, and there are multiple typos ('heay', 'fack-checking', 'verifiation'). Statistical significance or error bars across runs/seeds are not reported.

The MMLU-Pro experiments are limited: only three domains, only Llama-1B, small distillation set (1284 examples), and reliance on GPT-4o 'gold documents' to show an upper bound weakens the practical significance; retrieved-document results are unstable as acknowledged.

The filtering stage discards candidates irreversibly (false negatives reduce the effective candidate pool), and the interaction between filter recall and best-of-N performance at high N is not fully characterized for the harder Level-5 problems where gains vanish.

strengths: The paper addresses a relevant and well-motivated question: whether small language models can perform reliable self-verification for test-time scaling without relying on a large external verifier.

The proposed method (ToolV) is simple, clearly described, and composes naturally with existing verification paradigms (both PRMs and GenRMs), and the empirical evaluation covers multiple model families and scales (SmolLM2-360M, Qwen2.5-0.5B, Llama-3.2-1B) across three benchmarks (MATH500, GSM8K, MMLU-Pro).

The analysis sections are a positive aspect: category/level breakdowns, verifier-size ablations (Figure 8), filter-quality analysis with confusion matrices (Figure 10, Table 2), and data-efficiency experiments (Figure 11) go beyond a bare benchmark table.
The paper is honest about limitations (false-negative filtering, best-of-N scope) and provides detailed implementation and prompt information in the appendix, which supports reproducibility.
weaknesses: Limited novelty. The core idea—delegating memorization-heavy steps to external tools such as code interpreters—is well established (PAL, Toolformer, ToRA, tool-augmented reward modeling of Li et al. 2024, which the authors themselves cite). The contribution is essentially an application/combination of known components (tool use + verifier distillation + best-of-N) to the sLM self-verification setting, without a fundamentally new technique.

The theoretical analysis is shallow and largely restates prior results. Lemma 5.1 is a direct corollary of Theorem 1.1 in Brown et al. (2021), and Theorem 5.2's conclusion (I(X;θ|P)=0 when the tool computes the answer) is essentially immediate. Theorem 5.3 is adapted from Beirami et al. (2024). The formalism does not meaningfully connect to the actual method (e.g., the toy verifier model does not capture the code-generation failures that the authors themselves report in Section E.2 and Appendix F).

Some headline claims are weaker than presented. The claim that a 1B model 'outperforms the significantly larger Llama-3.1 8B model' compares scaled best-of-N with a distilled verifier against N=1 greedy decoding of the 8B model, which is not an apples-to-apples comparison; moreover, the method still depends on a substantially larger teacher (GPT-4o-mini and Qwen2.5-Math-PRM-7B) for distillation, which partially undercuts the 'no larger models' framing.

The computational cost of tool use is not accounted for. ToolV adds code generation (4 completions per solution) and execution to the verification pipeline, but the scaling curves plot accuracy only against N, treating the tool as free. A compute-matched or latency-matched comparison against baselines is needed to support the 'additional axis of scaling' claim.

The MMLU-Pro experiments are weak: only three domains, a single model, and the best configuration requires GPT-4o-generated 'gold documents', which is impractical and arguably not a realistic verifier setting; results with retrieved documents are noisy and gains are modest.

Generality is uncertain: the method assumes the relevant tool (code interpreter, retriever) is 'explicitly known' for each task, which is a strong prior that will not hold in open-ended settings. There is no evaluation on out-of-distribution tasks to test whether the distilled tool-use verifier generalizes.

Missing baselines: the paper does not compare against tool-integrated generation (e.g., generating solutions with code directly, PAL/ToRA-style) or against simply running code execution on the solution's arithmetic, which might achieve much of the benefit without distillation.

strengths: Clear and well-motivated research question: whether sLMs can self-verify under test-time scaling without relying on larger verifier models, addressing a practical gap in test-time compute scaling literature.

Empirically thorough evaluation: three model scales (SmolLM2-360M, Qwen2.5-0.5B, Llama-3.2-1B), two verifier paradigms (PRM and GenRM), three benchmarks (MATH500, GSM8K, MMLU-Pro), with appropriate baselines including majority voting, zero-shot GenRM, and distilled verifiers.

Strong headline result that is well supported: Llama-1B with ToolV outperforms Llama-8B greedy decoding on MATH500, and 1B GenRM + ToolV outperforms 8B GenRM alone, demonstrating that tool-based filtering can be more effective than scaling the verifier.

Useful diagnostic analyses: concept-proof experiment (Figure 1) isolating arithmetic verification difficulty as a function of N; confusion matrices showing ToolV mainly removes false positives; ablations over problem category/difficulty, verifier size, and distillation data scale; honest reporting of failure cases (symbolic equality bugs, false negatives) and limitations.
Generalization beyond math: adaptation of ToolV to fact-checking with retrieval on MMLU-Pro, including both retrieved and gold document settings to establish upper bounds.
Reproducibility is reasonably good: hyperparameters, prompts, teacher model, dataset splits, and evaluation protocol are detailed in the appendix.
weaknesses: Limited conceptual novelty: the core idea—delegating calculation-heavy verification to a code interpreter as a pre-filter before a reward model—is a fairly straightforward combination of well-known components (PAL/tool use + best-of-N with RM). Prior work on tool-augmented reward modeling (Li et al., 2024) and tool-integrated reasoning (Gou et al., 2024) is close, and the delta is primarily applying this to sLM self-verification.

The theoretical analysis is thin and largely repurposed: Lemma 5.1 directly cites Brown et al. (2021); Theorem 5.2 assumes an oracle tool achieving perfect verification accuracy (f = 1_{a+b=c}), an idealization far from the actual learned ToolV, whose recall is admittedly low (Table 3); Theorem 5.3 is essentially a known monotonicity property of best-of-N under imperfect verifiers (Beirami et al., 2024). The gap between the idealized theory and the empirical system is not bridged quantitatively.

No compute- or cost-matched comparison: ToolV adds code generation and execution per candidate (up to 4 completions per solution at N=64), so the inference cost is substantially higher than the distilled-PRM/GenRM baselines. Reporting accuracy alone at equal N does not establish that the gains hold under equal compute or latency budgets—an efficiency-focused paper should make this comparison explicit.

Some experimental results are modest and less convincing: GSM8K gains are small (as the authors note), MMLU-Pro results are unstable across N and limited to only three domains, and ToolV shows a dip at Level-5 problems and in Geometry, leaving the scope of applicability narrower than the abstract implies.

Design choices are under-justified: why a hard rejection filter rather than incorporating tool outputs into the verifier's context; the sensitivity to number of code completions and pass thresholds; and reliance on gpt-4o-mini as the distillation teacher for both the method and baselines is reasonable but the effect of teacher quality is unexamined.

Presentation has minor sloppiness (e.g., typos 'fack-checking', 'memorization-heay', 'verifiation') and several figures carry a large amount of information without error bars or variance reporting, which is important for best-of-N style evaluations.

strengths: Clear and well-motivated research question: whether small language models can serve as verifiers for test-time scaling without relying on larger verifier models, supported by a clean concept-proof experiment (Figure 1) that isolates the memorization bottleneck in verification.

The proposed two-stage T1 framework (tool-based filtering followed by RM-based scoring) is simple, modular, and shown to integrate with both PRMs and generative verifiers, with consistent gains across three small models (SmolLM2-360M, Qwen2.5-0.5B, Llama-3.2-1B) on GSM8K and MATH500.

Fair and thorough evaluation: comparisons against majority voting, zero-shot and distilled GenRM/PRM, and Themis; an ablation (Table 5, E.7) showing that a two-stage GenRM without tools does not yield the gains (ruling out a pure compute/multi-stage effect); a compute-budget normalization analysis (Figure 10, 11); confusion-matrix and precision/recall analysis of the filter; data-efficiency ablation; and per-category/per-level analysis that honestly reports where the method fails (Level 5, Geometry).

Theoretical analysis, while simple, is grounded in established results (Brown et al. 2021 memorization lower bound; Beirami et al. 2024 best-of-N analysis) and gives conceptual support to the empirical claims; proofs are provided in the appendix.
Good reproducibility posture: full hyperparameters, teacher models, prompts (D.1, D.2), dataset splits, exact per-N numbers in appendix tables, and a stated commitment to release code/scripts.
Honest limitations section that identifies the false-negative problem of rejection filtering and the restriction to parallel best-of-N scaling.
weaknesses: Limited conceptual novelty: the core idea of delegating arithmetic/factual checks to an interpreter or retriever is well-established (PAL, Toolformer, CRITIC, ToRA, tool-augmented reward modeling, Themis, PAD). The contribution is primarily an empirical study of applying this filtering idea to sLM verifiers in test-time scaling, which may be viewed as incremental.

The theoretical analysis is largely vacuous or derivative: Lemma 5.1 is a direct restatement of Brown et al. (2021); Theorem 5.2 assumes a perfect tool (f(a,b,c;θ,T) = 1_{a+b=c}) by construction, so the conclusion I(X;θ|P)=0 follows trivially from the assumption and says little about real, imperfect tools (which the paper itself shows have ~0.69-0.73 recall and nontrivial false-negative rates). Theorem 5.3 is a straightforward monotonicity computation.

The claimed '1B outperforms 8B' headline relies on comparing a small generator with 64-sample test-time scaling against a larger model with N=1 greedy decoding; while compute-budget comparisons are provided, the strongest claims are more nuanced than the abstract suggests.

Gains on the knowledge-intensive setting (MMLU-Pro subset, appendix) are modest and unstable with retrieved documents; performance is only clearly separated using GPT-4o-generated gold documents, which is not a deployable setup.

Method performance depends on teacher distillation from gpt-4o-mini and assumes the relevant tool (code interpreter, retriever) is known and appropriate for the task, limiting generality of the framework beyond domains with easily executable or retrievable verification signals.

Scale of evaluation is narrow: primarily math benchmarks plus a small MMLU-Pro subset in the appendix; no evaluation on harder settings (AIME/olympiad-level) where the paper cites prior scaling successes.

Writing has several typos and minor errors (e.g., 'fack-checking', 'verifiation', notation issues in Theorem 5.3 where conditions like q > 1−q are stated awkwardly), and the main-text theory section overstates the strength of what are idealized toy results.

strengths: Well-motivated problem: whether sLMs can serve as verifiers for test-time scaling is a relevant and underexplored question, and the motivating concept-proof experiment (Figure 1) cleanly demonstrates the memorization bottleneck in small-model verification.

The two-stage ToolV + RM framework is simple, general (applies to both PRMs and GenRMs), and empirically consistent: gains hold across three small models, two benchmarks, and both verifier types, with detailed per-N results in the appendix.

The paper proactively addresses compute overhead: it quantifies extra tokens, introduces a scaling-factor normalization of the x-axis, and shows ToolV remains competitive under an equal-compute comparison (Figure 10, Figure 11).

Useful ablations: two-stage vs. one-stage GenRM without tools (Table 5) rules out the trivial explanation that gains come from merely adding a verification stage; data-efficiency (Figure 15) and filter precision/recall analyses (Tables 3-4) are informative.
Reproducibility statements, hyperparameters, prompts, and case studies (success and failure) are provided, which supports transparency.
weaknesses: Limited novelty. The core idea — offloading arithmetic/fact-checking to a code interpreter or retriever during verification — is a straightforward combination of well-established components (program-aided verification, tool-augmented reward modeling e.g. Themis (Li et al., 2024), ToRA, CRITIC, PAD). The paper's own positioning concedes Themis already explored tool-augmented reward modeling; the delta here (applying it to <2B verifiers in best-of-N) is incremental.

The theoretical analysis is largely cosmetic. Lemma 5.1 is a direct restatement of Brown et al. (2021). Theorem 5.2 assumes by construction that the tool provides a perfect verification function f(a,b,c;T)=1_{a+b=c} and that θ is independent of X — from which I(X;θ|P)=0 follows tautologically, with no content about real tools or learned verifiers. Theorem 5.3 is elementary monotonicity of best-of-N in a binary toy setting. None of these results predict anything quantitative or testable about the actual system; the paper itself admits the results are 'conceptual illustrations'.

A critical missing baseline: tool-integrated generation. If the sLM can generate correct verification code (as ToolV requires), one should compare against directly generating solutions with code execution (PAL/ToRA-style), or at minimum running the interpreter on the solution's final arithmetic. The paper never clarifies why verification-time tool use dominates generation-time tool use at equal compute.

Cost accounting is incomplete. The 1.14x scaling-factor argument counts output tokens only, ignoring teacher-model distillation cost, code-execution latency/infrastructure, and the fact that GPT-4o-mini (the teacher) could itself verify candidates directly — a natural and cheap baseline that is not compared.

Benchmark scope is narrow: essentially MATH500 and GSM8K, both math-centric where a code interpreter is nearly an oracle for calculation. The MMLU-Pro extension (appendix) shows unstable results and relies on GPT-4o-generated gold documents to look good, weakening the generality claim. Level-5 problems and Geometry show degradation (Figure 6), suggesting the method's benefit is confined to computation-heavy mid-difficulty problems.

Headline claims are somewhat over-stated: 'a Llama-3.2 1B outperforms the significantly larger Llama-3.1 8B' compares best-of-64 with tool-filtered verification against a single greedy 8B pass, which is a compute-unmatched comparison; absolute accuracies in some settings are very low (e.g., ~10% for SmolLM2 on MATH500), making practical significance unclear.

Some design choices are under-justified: using 'pass if any of 4 generated codes passes' for math but 'pass only if all 4 rationales pass' for fact-checking appears ad hoc; the sensitivity of results to these rules is not analyzed.

strengths: Well-motivated and clearly framed research question: whether sLMs can act as reliable verifiers under test-time scaling, with a clean concept-proof experiment (Figure 1) that convincingly demonstrates the memorization bottleneck in small verifiers.
The proposed two-stage design (tool-based filtering followed by RM-based scoring) is simple, general, and integrates with both PRMs and GenRMs; the framework is clearly formalized (Equations 3-4).

Comprehensive and honest empirical evaluation: consistent gains across three model families (SmolLM2-360M, Qwen2.5-0.5B, Llama-3.2-1B), two verifier types, and two benchmarks, with full exact numbers in appendix tables, confusion matrices, category/level analysis, data-efficiency ablations, and a two-stage-without-tool ablation (Table 5) that isolates the contribution of tool integration rather than extra compute.

The compute-budget discussion (Section 6.4, Figure 10) directly addresses the key confound that ToolV adds tokens, comparing against larger verifiers and re-plotting with scaled x-axes; this strengthens the central claim that 1B + ToolV beats 8B verifiers.
Good coverage of related work and transparent reporting of limitations (false negatives from the filter, parallel-scaling-only scope), including failure cases with concrete examples.
Theoretical framing, though simple, is grounded in established results (Brown et al. 2021; Beirami et al. 2024) and the paper is upfront that it is conceptual rather than a tight bound on practice.
weaknesses: Limited novelty: tool-integrated verification and tool-augmented reward modeling already exist (Themis, Li et al. 2024; tool-augmented RM); the main contribution is essentially applying tool filtering to small verifiers with a filter-then-score ordering, which is an incremental design choice rather than a new capability or training method.

The theoretical analysis is largely decorative: Lemma 5.1 directly restates Brown et al. (2021), Theorem 5.2's proof assumes theta is chosen independently of X (making the result nearly vacuous), and Theorem 5.3 relies on a binary-output, symmetric generator toy setting from Beirami et al. (2024). The gap between these idealizations and the actual system (multi-step code generation, 4-completion voting, filtering rules) is large.

The headline claim of 'verification without larger models' is partially undermined by the method's dependence on distillation from a strong external teacher (GPT-4o-mini) for both ToolV and the reward model; reproducibility depends on a commercial API whose outputs may change, and the 'small model' framing would be stronger with a self-improvement or open-teacher setup.

The compute-budget normalization is crude: scaling the x-axis by a token-count factor (1.14x) ignores latency, execution cost, and the fact that code execution is sequential and non-parallelizable; a wall-clock or FLOP-based comparison would be more convincing.

Evaluation scope is narrow: main results are on MATH500/GSM8K (math only); the knowledge-intensive MMLU-Pro experiment is relegated to the appendix, uses only 3 domains with a minimal retrieval setup, and shows unstable results with retrieved documents. Geometry and Level-5 problems show regressions, which limits the claimed generality.

Theoretical result on filtering (Theorem 5.3) justifies monotonicity in verifier noise, but the paper does not empirically measure how the tool filter's false-negative rate (noted as non-trivial in E.3: recall is low) interacts with the weighted Best-of-N aggregation when all candidates are filtered out; this failure mode deserves explicit treatment.

Writing quality issues remain: typos ('fack-checking', 'verifiation'), an inconsistency where GSM8K is described as 'graduate-level arithmetic' in Figure 5's caption, and some results (e.g., MMLU-Pro gold-doc setup) feel under-specified for full reproducibility.
